title: FIDE World U7-U17 Rapid and Blitz Championships 2026 Egypt: Registration continues
summary: The International Chess Federation (FIDE) and the Egyptian Chess Federation are pleased to invite all the member federations to the 2026 FIDE World U7-U17 Rapid and Blitz Championships. The event will take place in Cairo, Egypt, from December 8 (arrival) to December 15 (departure), 2026. The participants will compete across six age categories: Under 7, Under 9, Under 11, Under 13, Under 15, and Under 17, with separate Open and Girls sections. Players who secured first place in the previous edition of the FIDE World Rapid & Blitz Cadets & Youth Championships (U9–U17 age groups) are granted the personal right to participate in the corresponding (or higher) age category, provided they meet the age requirement as of January 1, 2026. FIDE Member Federations may register an unlimited number of players and accompanying officials/persons. The registration deadline is November 1, 2026. Invitation, regulations, schedule (PDF) Registration details Registration form: https://forms.gle/sJW3H1QfS5FZ3kqE8 Email: youthrapidblitz@fide.com  Official website: https://youthrapidblitz2026.fide.com

title: FIDE Announces Open Call for Commission Nominations
summary: Following the election of the new FIDE leadership, we are entering a new chapter of our work –  building on what has been achieved, continuing the projects that have proven successful, and developing new initiatives that can make FIDE and chess even more effective, innovative, and impactful. FIDE Commissions and Committees play a vital role in this process. Their expertise, commitment, and connection with the chess community are essential to turning our strategic priorities into meaningful action. With this in mind, FIDE is launching an open process for nominations to all non-elected positions within FIDE Commissions/Committees. All FIDE National Federations, affiliated organizations, and Continental Federations are invited to suggest candidates who can contribute their expertise, experience, and ideas to the work of the Commissions/Committees. Individuals who wish to put themselves forward are also welcome to apply. In such cases, candidates should be aware that, if appointed, they will need to obtain the support of their respective National Federation. How to apply Applications should be submitted via the form below by October 20, 2026. Alternatively, the application can be submitted by email. In this case, the applicant should complete the attached Excel form and send it to office@fide.com. Any candidate may be applying for several positions, filling in a separate application for each of the preferred positions.  Each application should indicate: •⁠ ⁠the preferred Commission(s)/Committee(s);•⁠ ⁠the preferred position — Chair, Secretary or Member;•⁠ ⁠CV and a brief justification for the preferred position;•⁠ ⁠the candidate’s relevant professional experience and expertise;•⁠ ⁠the contribution the candidate intends to make to the work of the Commission/Committee; and•⁠ ⁠suggestions for improving or further developing the Commission’s/Committee’s work.  We encourage candidates not only to present their experience but also to share their vision of how the Commission/Committee can contribute to FIDE’s future priorities and serve the chess community more effectively. Building strong and diverse teams Following the open application process, the new nominations will be considered with the aim of creating strong, effective and diverse Commission/Committee teams. The selection process will take into account, in particular: •⁠ ⁠professional expertise and relevant experience;•⁠ ⁠regional representation and diversity;•⁠ ⁠gender balance; and•⁠ ⁠the candidate’s ability to make a meaningful contribution to the Commission’s/Committee’s work. The current list of non-elected commissions and their respective areas of responsibility can be consulted in the FIDE Handbook:FIDE Handbook – Non-Elected Commissions

title: Respect over results: Sebastian Poltorak and Tin Jingyao receive Gligoric Trophy 2026
summary:
Press release by FIDE

Following a review of the nominations for the 2026 Svetozar Gligorić Trophy, the FIDE Gligorić Trophy Award Commission has decided to award the trophy to two recipients:

Sebastian Poltorak (Poland) – For his exemplary sportsmanship during the 2025 European Chess Club Cup. In his game against Aleksandar Inđjić, when his opponent became unwell and had to leave the playing hall for medical reasons, Poltorak agreed to a draw rather than seeking a competitive advantage from the situation.

GM Tin Jingyao (Singapore) – For his exemplary fair play during the 2025 Almaty Region Open (Qonayev Cup). In round six, his opponent arrived after the default time due to heavy traffic. Although Tin Jingyao was entitled to claim a win by forfeit, he graciously chose to allow the game to be played.

The Commission considers both cases to be exceptional examples of fair play and sportsmanship, where respect for the opponent prevailed over the competitive result.

The Svetozar Gligoric Trophy is an award given by FIDE to the individual who displays exemplary behavior promoting the spirit of fair play and sportsmanship in chess.

To be eligible for the Svetozar Gligoric Trophy 2026, candidates must have demonstrated the following accomplishments during the period from September 2024 to September 2026 :

Outstanding gesture or action of sportsmanship during a sporting event.

Outstanding contribution to the popularization of values and principles of Fair Play.

Outstanding initiatives on enforcement of integrity and high ethical values.

The Svetozar Gligoric Trophy recognizes sportsmen who exercise the fundamental values of fair play both during and beyond the game. It represents a mindset rather than mere behavior, rooted in the following concepts:

Fairness – To enjoy the victory is not enough. Triumph must include fairness and honesty.

Respect – Written rules are mandatory. Unwritten rules of respect to all are obligatory.

Friendship – Rivalry in sports does not exclude friendship.

Team spirit – A genuine consideration for teammates.

Equality – Competing on equal terms is essential.

Tolerance – The willingness and ability to accept what you may not agree with.

Care – True champions care about each other.

The winner of the Svetozar Gligoric Trophy is selected by the FIDE Gligoric Trophy Award Commission .

Please note that this award pertains solely to nominee's accomplishments during the period September 2024 – September 2026 and is not a recognition of lifelong career accomplishments.

The Commission's decision is final and not subject to appeal. The members of the Commission are not required to give justification unless they choose to do so.

title: Learning strategy from Bent Larsen
summary:
Turning structural imbalances into active play

Bent Larsen was one of the strongest players outside the Soviet Union during the 1960s and 1970s, combining an adventurous approach to the openings with an ability to handle unusual middlegame structures. The Danish grandmaster was rarely content merely to follow established paths. His games frequently featured early deviations from theory, ambitious pawn advances and positions in which long-term strategic considerations were closely connected with concrete tactical possibilities.

The 20 th volume of the ChessBase Master Class series examines these different aspects of his play. Dorian Rogozenco, Mihail Marin, Karsten Müller and Oliver Reeh cover Larsen's openings, strategic play, endgames and tactical ability, while Peter Heine Nielsen contributes a separate chapter devoted to memories and impressions of Denmark's most celebrated chess player. The course also contains collections of Larsen's games and additional training material.

Born in 1935, Larsen emerged as Denmark's strongest player while still in his teens. He won the national championship six times and earned the GM title following his performance at the 1956 Chess Olympiad in Moscow, where he took the individual gold medal on first board.

His most successful period came during the 1960s. Larsen won the Interzonal tournaments of Amsterdam 1964 and Sousse 1967 and qualified repeatedly for the Candidates matches. For several years he and Bobby Fischer were generally regarded as the leading Western challengers to the Soviet players who dominated elite chess at the time.

Larsen's reputation for originality was well-earned. He was prepared to employ openings that other leading grandmasters considered unconventional, with 1.b3 becoming particularly closely associated with his name. Yet reducing his chess to eccentric opening choices would give an incomplete picture. Much of his success came from his understanding of imbalanced positions and his willingness to accept structural concessions when they provided useful squares, active pieces or attacking prospects.

These elements form an important part of the strategy section of the Master Class volume. Rather than presenting Larsen simply as an attacking player, the course looks at the positional ideas that allowed him to create the conditions for later tactical play.

A lesson from Monte Carlo

One of the games featured in the strategy material is Larsen's encounter with Romanian grandmaster Florin Gheorghiu at Monte Carlo 1968. The tournament came during one of Larsen’s strongest periods: he finished first with 9½/13, half a point ahead of former world champion Mikhail Botvinnik, while Vasily Smyslov (also a former world champion) and Vlastimil Hort shared third place on 8½ points.

In a position with all six major pieces still on the board, Larsen repeatedly improved the coordination of his pieces, first demonstrating why his superior structure was a bigger trump than Gheorghiu's extra pawn and then creating decisive activity on the kingside.

Larsen v. Gheorghiu

White has the better structure and piece coordination, but Black's extra pawn at least partly compensates for these aspects. As a general evaluation, White's position is preferable, but he needs to play accurately in order to convert it into a win.

Larsen here played the strong 23.h4! , attempting gaining the initiative on the kingside. Going for 23.Rxd6 would have been premature due to 23...Rxd6 24.Rxd6 Qb1+ 25.Kg2 Qe4+, with good drawing chances for Black.

There followed 23...Qe5! 24.b3 Rc8?! (a bit slow; better is to go for counterplay with 24...a4!, intending to double the rooks on the b-file) 25.Rd5!

Once again, Larsen focuses on piece coordination and activity. Keeping the pawn with 25.e3?! allows Black to regroup in time with 25...Rc5.

25...Qxe2 26.h5! Rc2 27.Rf1

Black's 27...Qe4? here was a crucial mistake. Instead, he should have defended g6 with the rather unexpected 27...Qe8, intending to transfer one of his rooks to g4 in order to get counterplay (with the queen on e4, this is not possible).

Larsen duly made the most of his opponent's inaccuracy: 28.Rxa5 a6 29.Ra4! (gaining a tempo by attacking the badly placed queen on e4) Qe8 30.Rg4

The white rook has been transferred from d5 to g4, increasing the pressure on the kingside. Had Black played ...Qe8 at the right moment, the g4-square could have been occupied by a black rook instead, with good drawing chances.

30...Qf8 31.Qe3?! Placing the queen on e3 keeps White's clear advantage, but he could have broken through at once with 31.Rxg6+ hxg6 32.Qxg6+ Kh8 33.Qxc2, and Black is doomed.

31...Rbc6 32.hxg6 hxg6 33.Rxg6 Kf7

With the queen on the open e-file and the rook on f1 ready to join the attack, the rest was simple for Larsen: 34.Rg4 R2c5 35.Qd3 Re5 36.f4 Re8 37.Qd5+ Ke7 38.Re1+ 1-0

The complete lesson

title: Six-way tie in the lead after two rounds in Fagernes
summary:
Three Norwegians among the early leaders

The Fagernes International Autumn Tournament is under way in Norway, with the GM Swiss group serving as the main event of the festival. The competition is being played from 3 to 11 October at the Scandic Valdres hotel in Fagernes, around 187 kilometres north of Oslo. Hans Olav Lahlum is the main organiser, working in cooperation with Sotra Sjakklubb.

The GM group is being contested over ten rounds in nine days, a format designed in part to provide greater flexibility for players pursuing title norms. The schedule includes a double-round day (on Tuesday), while the remaining days feature one classical game. The ten-round structure allows norm performances to be calculated over different nine-game stretches in certain circumstances.

The time control is 100 minutes for the first 40 moves, followed by 40 minutes for the remainder of the game, with a 30-second increment from move one. The section is open to titled players and to competitors meeting the specified rating requirements of 2000, or 1900 for women. First prize in the GM group is €3,000.

A number of experienced grandmasters are competing in the section. Norwegian champion Elham Amar is the top seed with a rating of 2567, followed by Kazakhstan's Rinat Jumabayev on 2564 and Norway's Frode Olav Olsen Urkedal on 2554. Abhijeet Gupta, G. B. Harshavardhan and Krishnan Sasikiran are the next three players on the starting list, while Aksel Bu Kvaloy and German rising star Christian Gloeckler are both rated 2515.

Top seed Elham Amar played black against Krishnan Ritvik in Saturday's first round (0-1) | Photo: Anna Ovidia Young

After the opening two rounds, six players share first place with perfect scores. Sweden's Tiger Hillarp Persson (2417) is joined on 2/2 by Aksel Bu Kvaloy (2515) of Norway, Christian Gloeckler (2515) of Germany, Harika Dronavalli (2453) of India, Frode Olav Olsen Urkedal (2554) of Norway and Mads Vestby-Ellingsen (2390) of Norway.

Fagernes has become a regular venue for international chess in Norway. Lahlum has organised tournaments there since 2014, following earlier events in Gausdal and Oslo, and the 2026 autumn competition forms part of the Norges Grand Prix 2026–27 circuit.

All games from the GM group are being broadcast online with a 15-minute delay. The tournament concludes on Sunday 11 October, when the tenth and final round will be played in the morning.

Haugen v. Myagmarsuren

The all-Norwegian round-one battle between Lars Haugen and Evsuld Myagmarsuren ended rather abruptly after White faltered by playing 24.Rf1?

Though placing the rook on the f-file seems to help White to deal with the threat of a potential attack on the weak f2-spot, it was necessary to start by displacing the black queen on g5 after either 24.Rg3 or 24.Qd2.

After the text move, Black wins in style: 24...fxe4 25.Rg3 (too late) Rxf2!

White is doomed. Resignation came after 26.Rxf2 Qc1+ (playing Rg3 or Qd2 in the first diagrammed position would have prevented the black queen from infiltrating on this diagonal) 27.Qf1 Bxf2 28.Kxf2 Rf8+

The other rook joins the fun and it is game over. Importantly, the pawn on e4 prevents the white rook from defending on f3.
